does: Ties a bird or a joint into a compact shape, so that it cooks evenly and keeps its form.

intro.what: Trussing ties a bird or joint into a compact shape before cooking.
intro.why: It teaches you to control the outline with snug string while avoiding pressure that cuts into the flesh.

how: Tuck the wing tips under the back of the bird.
Pass a length of string under the tail, cross it over the ends of the drumsticks and pull them together.
Run the string along the sides, between the legs and the breast, and tie it at the neck.
For a joint, tie loops of string along it at even spaces, snug but not tight.

cues.text: A neat, plump shape with nothing sticking out, and string that is snug without cutting in.

mistakes.mistake: Tying so tightly that the string cuts into the flesh and squeezes the juice out.
mistakes.fix: Pull it snug and no more.

mistakes.mistake: Leaving the legs splayed, so that the breast dries before the thighs are done.
mistakes.fix: Draw the legs in against the breast.

quiz.question: What is the shaping aim of trussing?
choices: A spread-out form with every limb extended.
A compact form with loose parts drawn in.
A deeply compressed shape with string grooves.
quiz.because: Drawing loose parts toward the body gives the piece a more contained outline.

quiz.question: What happens to the wing tips in this bird-trussing method?
choices: Pull them outward away from the body.
Tie them tightly across the exposed breast.
quiz.because: Tucking keeps the tips from projecting beyond the compact shape.

quiz.question: Which appearance suggests appropriate string tension?
choices: Snug string that does not cut into the flesh.
Deep grooves where each loop bites in.
Loose loops hanging away from the surface.
quiz.because: The string should support the outline without compressing and marking the flesh deeply.

quiz.question: The string cuts into the flesh. What should change?
choices: Pull it snug with less tension.
Add more tight loops over the same grooves.
quiz.because: More pressure is not needed once the string holds the shape; reducing tension limits cutting.
